It is well known that by subjecting mix-
tures of carbonic oxid and hydrogen to the
action of catalyzers at high pressure it is pos-

_ sible to obtain hydrocarbons or oxygenated

§ organic compounds (methane, methyl alco-

hol, higher alcohols, aldehydes, acids, ethers,

_ ete.) in proportions and with yields which

differ greatly according to the experimental

conditions and the nature of the catalyzing

10 substances. Certain impurities, present even

in relatively small quantity in the catalyzers,

may radically alter the course of the synthe-

sis; they may, for example, produce methane
instead of alcohols. - |

15 On account of the very great variety of

_ products which can be obtained from a single

gaseous mixture under the same conditions of

_ , temperature and pressure, it is evident that

choice of the catalyzer is of the utmost im-

20 portance, seeing that the catalyzer is the

fundamental factor whereon.all processes are

--based which seek to obtain liquid products
of greater value from water gas. -

Many catalyzers have been proposed for the

25 synthesis of methyl alcohol. These cataly-
_ zers, all of which are artificial, are ordinarily
obtained by the wet method, and must under-
go a preliminary filtration, washing and dry-
ing treatment, as well as mechanical treat-
30 ments for agglomerating them in a suitable
compact form. Some require careful prep-
aration, and others have to undergo a reduc.
tion treatment previous to being used. Cat-
alyzers have also been proposed embodying
35 as a support or carrier inert materials such
_as asbestus which dilute the active catalyzer ;
as well as other catalyzers which are obtained
by the addition of foreign substances which
act as agglomerants on the mixtures of oxids,
40 themselves pulverulent and, consequently, un-
suitable for filling the catalytic space wherein
gases circulate, often at high speed. Further-
more, many of the catalyzers proposed are
very expensive, particularly those obtained by
45 the addition, as activants, of compounds of
certain rare metals such as uranium, thorium,
cobalt, ete. — ae
The following process for the synthesis of
methyl alcohol and other organic products is
50 based on the use, as catalyzers, of certain -

Smithsonite, which is a mineral consisting 55
chiefly of zinc carbonate, as is well known, is
extremely active. The raw crystalline min-
eral, although containing yellowish, reddish,
brown and greenish parts due to impurities
in the gangue, and although containing for- 60
elen matter such as iron, manganese, lime and
‘silea, can, after having’ been roughly broken
up, be introduced directly into the catalyz-
ing towers. When preheated to a tempera-
ture close to 400° C., it is ready to be used 65
tor the synthesis. Even white smithsonite,
which is purer and which has a coneretion-
ary, crystalline appearance, possess an in-
tense catalytic property.
Calcined smithsonite cannot, from the 70
point of view of catalysis, be considered as
ordinary zinc oxid. This is demonstrated by
its extraordinarily high activity which must
be attributed to the presence of numerous:
substances, intimately distributed in the 75
form of homogencous solid solutions, or of
compounds which cannot be obtained arti-
ficially. Even the artificial mixtures pro-
duced by precipitating the carbonates of
zinc simultaneously with those of manganese, 80
iron, calcium, etc., are less active than natural |
smithsonite. It is known that diffusion in
the solid. state at temperatures much lower
than the fusing point ocurs only very slowly.
In natural smithsonite, these solid solutions 85
have had time to form during the extremely __
long geological ages by crystallization of
very dilute solutions; probably under high
temperatures and pressures, all of which
form a composite of conditions which cannot 90
be reproduced artificially.
_ smithsonite can’ be heated to 400°-450°
C., before use, or it may even be introduced
just as it is into the synthesis apparatus.
Quantitative comparisons show that with 95
the same conditions of catalytic space, tem-—
perature and gas velocity, mineral smithson-
Ite has an enormously greater activity than
that of carbonate or oxid of zine and of
chromium (obtained according to the metli- 100

ods described by Patart and by “ Badische
Soda und Anilin Fab.”) which is ordinarily
considered to be one of the best catalyzers.
Tt should be noted that the chief impurities.
5 present in smithsonite, particularly the iron,
are not harmful but, on the contrary, prob-
ably increase the catalytic property. Cer-
tain grades of green smithsonite, owing ‘to
the presence of ferrous carbonate in iso-
10 morphous mixture with the zine carbonate,
can even be used advantageously for the
synthesis of the methyl alcohol without in-
volving the contemporaneous formation of.
. methane © | | |
15 A gas has been treated which was obtained
‘by the action of electrolytic oxygen and
steam on carbon by eliminating, by washing,
a part of the carbonic anhydride. This gas-
- @ous mixture, containing nearly 30% of
20 carbonic oxid, 7% of carbonic anhydride,
more than 60% of hydrogen and only traces
of oxygen and nitrogen, and being subjected
to a pressure of 260-300 atmospheres and to
a temperature of nearly 400° C., gave an in-
25 crease of 20% in the yield for each passage,
per liter of gross:catalytic space, and with, a
velocity of the gas of nearly 15 cubic meters
per hour, compared to the yield when zinc
- oxide or carbonate or chromium oxide or

| 80 carbonate is used as the catalytic agent. The

condensed liquid is composed principally of
methyl alcohol, and it.contains only very
small amounts of water. Very highly puri-
, fied methyl alcohol can then be obtained by
— 35 simple distillation. — | oe
The yield remains fairly high even at
temperatures exceeding 400° C. or somewhat
lower. It is satisfactory at 340-350° C., and
at pressures slightly higher than 100 atmo-
49 spheres. -

- The present catalyzer, due to its compact-
ness, possesses the advantageous property of
not being subject to localized overheating,

and of having a peculiar stability; and even
45 sfter a prolonged operation with unpurified
gases, its catalytic activity is not lessened in
the.slightest.
Given its remarkable activity, its low cost,
-. its valuable mechanical properties, and its
59 stability, and the fact that it does not re-
. quire any preliminary treatment, the min-
eral can be used to great advantage in the
_ gynthesis of methyl alcohol.
_ Moreover, in the case where the gaseous
55 mixture circulates very slowly, it is possible
- to obtain, besides methyl alcohol, other oxy-
genated organic compounds of great value.
